headline: Wreck 6-8-2 in 130 feet: sea bass to 5 pounds, bluefin working the Mud Hole lumps
subhead: A warm filament pushing toward the Hudson and Wilmington approaches has mahi and yellowfin within range, while the reef wrecks keep filling coolers with jumbo bass.
body_markdown:
Sixty-two feet of water over the top of Wreck 6-8-2, dead calm Tuesday morning, and the sounder painted a solid red-orange smear that told me everything before the first bait hit bottom. That's the kind of return I've been chasing on this piece of structure since I first punched the numbers into a loran box twenty years ago, and it hasn't let me down yet in July. Sea bass to five pounds came off that wreck on Gulp Grubs in white and chartreuse, fished on a high-low rig with 4-ounce bank sinkers to hold bottom against the current. The jumbos are sitting tight to the wreckage itself, not scattered on the sand around it, so if your drift walks you off the numbers, reel up and reset. I lost count of the shorts we threw back before the keepers started stacking, but that's a good problem to have this time of year.

Axel Carlson Reef and Sea Girt Reef are both fishing the same way right now — deep down in the structure, not up on top. Clam and squid strips on bucktail teasers are outproducing straight bait rigs for me this week, especially in the mid-morning when the sun gets up and the fish tuck deeper into the shade of the wreckage. Shrewsbury Rocks has been more hit or miss — I had one drift there Thursday that produced eight keepers in twenty minutes and then went dead for the next hour. That's typical for the Rocks in midsummer; the bait pods move through in waves and the bass follow them, so if you find the pod, work it hard before it slides off.

Offshore, this is shaping up to be one of the better midrange tuna stretches I've seen in a few years. The Mud Hole lumps have been holding bluefin in that 27-to-46-inch slot class consistently since the trophy fishery closed on the 3rd, and the two-fish recreational limit means guys are still going home with fish without having to grind through a full spread all day. I've been running green machines and cedar plugs off the riggers with a naked ballyhoo down the shotgun, trolling the deeper edges of the lumps where the temp break holds — the water's been clean and blue out there, not the usual green chop you fight through in a normal July. Barnegat Ridge has produced sporadically for the smaller bluefin class as well, mostly early, before the wind fills in out of the southwest by midday.

We flagged this last week — said the warm-water filaments pushing toward the Hudson and Wilmington canyon approaches would put decent yellowfin and mahi within range of the Jersey fleet, and that's exactly what's playing out. Boats running out to those canyon edges are finding mahi stacked on anything floating — lobster pot buoys, loose weed lines, the odd pallet or trap marker. Dink lines with small hookless teasers followed by a naked ballyhoo or a green-and-yellow feather have been the play once you spot the color change or a bird working low over the surface. Yellowfin are mixing in on the same water, and the size class has been ticking up slightly from what we were seeing two weeks ago — nothing giant yet, but a step in the right direction if this stable high pressure holds through the week like it's supposed to.

No bonito yet in our zone. Water temps up around Montauk and Block Island are creeping into the range where they typically show, but I haven't had a confirmed fish crossed off in the Mud Hole or along the Ridge. Worth keeping an eye on temperature breaks over the next couple weeks, especially if this offshore warmth keeps pushing inshore, but I wouldn't plan a trip around it yet.

Tog season's closed through the summer, so that's a fall conversation — I'll start pulling my blackfish numbers back out once the water starts to turn in September. Cod's the same story; not worth chasing structure for them until the water cools off considerably.

Looking ahead, if this high-pressure pattern holds through the weekend like it's forecast to, I'd expect the canyon bite to keep building rather than fade — the Hooper-style warm filaments don't usually collapse overnight, and mahi numbers tend to climb through late July as more weed and debris gets pushed into range. On the inshore side, I'd keep working the reef wrecks early before the wind builds, and I wouldn't be surprised if the Mud Hole lumps keep producing slot bluefin right through the week as long as the bait stays put on those temperature edges. If I had one trip to make this weekend, I'd run out to check the Hudson approach for color and bait before committing to a full canyon day — but I'd have Wreck 6-8-2 as my fallback if the offshore water looks wrong.
